His influence on Hollywood is comparable to Einstein’s influence on Physics. I love all his films and one thing I always notice is how well the actors are staged within the frame and movement of the scene. Watch High and Low and Ikiru next

He influenced most of the great filmmakers of the late 70s to now. Spielberg, Scorsese, etc. A lot of Star Wars is inspired by Kurosawa films.

He's also a master of shot composition and blocking. A lot can be learned from him.

I'm sort of ashamed to admit that I've never really been captivated by his films with the exception of throne of blood and rashomon. I can appreciate them objectively and acknowledge their importance but there's plenty of other Japanese films I enjoy more.

There are some directors that I love where a single element of their style really stands out because they are more idiosyncratic. For example the cold, fluidity of Fincher, the gorgeous camera work of Ophüls, or the ability to direct kinetic action cleanly like George Miller. However, Kurosawa (for me) doesn't have a single stand-out element of his work that makes him so great, but its instead that he has more of a "silent" style where every decision just adds up to make the most compelling and impactful story. He's very similar to John Ford in that way because I couldn't list the thematic or stylistic choices that make them a 100% unique vision, but I know that their movies flow so well and every aspect of the filmmaking is in service of the story. 

There was a [great video breakdown](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LC8KYm85zig&ab_channel=CineFix-IGNMoviesandTV) of the blocking from a scene High and Low. I think it did a great job breaking down the thousand small decisions that aren't flashy or attention seeking that build a wonderfully told story. For what its worth I would also highly recommend High and Low because it shows that Kurosawa can do a lot more than just period-piece samurai movies

As with most hugely influential filmmakers, his techniques have become so normalised that to watch them now means it’s likely you won’t appreciate them fully. 

Try watching a documentary or reading a book about his films before watching any more. It might just help you understand better how innovative he was.

It's a few different things for me, a combination of his blocking, camera movements and composition, and editing. His blocking is often so theatrical and heightened, he uses the actors movement as a storytelling tool in a way not many do today. His camera movements are precise and, for lack of a better word, cinematic. They sweep, they push in, they pull back, all as needed by the story, never just for flourish or style. Think of that rotating shot in Seven Samurai where all the spears are pointed up, and the camera rotates around them as they speak to the farmers. Lastly his editing, he is great at getting the audience to look at an action or area of the screen, and then cutting around that action, quickly enough we sometimes don't realize it's happened. To do all these things well enough to still be revered today in the 50s and 60s is a wonderful feat. High and Low and Ikiru are two of my favorites of his.

Of the three you mentioned I've only seen seven samurai.   I really liked, but is pretty slow
I say give Yojimbo, and High and Low a shot. Yojimbo is quick and fun. High and Low is contemporary crime movie.

Try High and Low or Ikiru. He is very versatile, and you've seem 2 of his Samurai masterpieces - maybe you don't like Samurai films. Dreams is definitely not an essential Kurosawa film, but it is pretty cool.

Yojimbo was the first film I saw of his that I truly enjoyed and wanted to watch again. High and Low is excellent too, the pacing of that story had me totally sucked in.

Like a few others who have commented, I absolutely adore Ozu but don’t love Kurosawa. I don’t think it’s an uncommon taste profile to have even among cinephiles. But I do recall my college professor who loves Kurosawa waxing lyrical about kurosawa’s contribution to filmic language. Like Eisenstein, he thought up a lot of the ways certain emotions or ideas can be communicated especially effectively in film. If Eisenstein is all about montage and the synergy from the collision of two or more images, Kurosawa is about the language of light and dark and the movement of light. There are several great examples from seven samurai alone. There are shots of just light shimmering or shifting, not gratuitously placed but carrying meaning that enhances the narrative.

Haha yeah Ozu is the master filmmaker I think of when I think of Japanese cinema. I know it's been endlessly debated but the vse shot in late spring is still so provocative and always gets me thinking. Such a gentle and human filmmaker. I think more recently though hanna-bi is an all time favourite and love anything but kiyoshi kurosawa. Haven't seen castle in the sky but onibaba and kwaidan are both great. Horror in general the Japanese have such a unique take on. Woman in the dunes comes to mind too.
Some great points and I get the John Ford comparisons but I adore Ford's work and never clicked with Kurosawa's. I guess sometimes it does just come down to personal taste. Even with the masters.

You feel it, or you don't. 

I had the opportunity to see Ran in the theater. It was one of the greatest experiences of my life.

I was overwhelmed by the vivid, colorful violence. The scope. The operatic drama painted across this vast canvas.

If you're talking about these three films specifically, the only one I really liked was Ran. King Lear has always been my favorite Shakespeare play, and I think Ran is by far the best adaptation of it. On the other hand, I felt that Seven Samurai is a bit too long and I appreciate it more than I like it.

If you're asking about Kurosawa in general, I think his greatest strength is his consistency. Throughout the 50's and early 60's, Kurosawa released a remarkable number of great films. Seeing that you enjoyed the three you've seen so far, it is only logical to delve deeper into one the best filmographies of the 20th century.

Four films I will recommend are Ikiru, Yojimbo, Stray Dog, and High and Low. These film are plot-driven with good character depth, they are some of his best films in my opinion and they somewhat easy to get.
